title: Fischer trades his best piece
summary: Buenos Aires, 1971: Fischer swaps a beautiful knight for a bishop because the endgame that follows is easier to win.

steps.title: Buenos Aires, 1971
steps.text: In 1971 Fischer tore through the Candidates matches, beating Mark Taimanov and Bent Larsen without losing a game. In the final he met Tigran Petrosian, a former world champion who was almost impossible to beat. This is game seven of that final. Fischer won the match and the right to play Spassky for the title.
steps.narration: Buenos Aires, 1971. Fischer against the former world champion Tigran Petrosian, with a world championship match as the prize.

steps.title: Fischer – Petrosian, Candidates final, Buenos Aires 1971
steps.text: The queens come off early. Black is left with two isolated pawns on a6 and d5, and Fischer starts pressing on them. Watch how simple every move looks.
steps.narration: The queens are traded early. Watch Fischer press on Black's weak pawns with simple moves.

notes.text: 13...Qxa4: the queens come off. Black has isolated pawns on a6 and d5: no pawn next to them can protect them.
17.Bxe7: Fischer trades the dark bishops. His remaining bishop will be better than Black's.
19.Nc5: the knight lands on a great square, hitting a6 and the bishop.
22.Nxd7+!: Fischer trades his beautiful knight for Black's bishop. His bishop against Black's knight, with pawns on both wings, is an endgame a bishop loves.
24...Rd6, after 24.Rc7, a white rook stands on the seventh rank.
26.Kf2: in the endgame the king joins the fight.
29...d4+: Petrosian pushes his pawn, but now it is far from home and cut off.
31.Ree7: both white rooks are on the seventh rank, right next to the black king.
34.Bc4: the bishop joins, and Black's king is trapped on the back rank. Petrosian resigned.

guesses.prompt: Fischer just traded his knight for the bishop. The rook on a1 is doing nothing. Give it a job.
guesses.hint: There is an open file in the middle of the board, leading to the seventh rank.
guesses.why: 23.Rc1 takes the open c-file. Next the rook goes to c7, on the seventh rank, where it ties Black's pieces down.

guesses.prompt: Black's passed pawn on d4 gives check. Where should the king go?
guesses.hint: In an endgame, the best piece to stop a passed pawn is the king, standing right in front of it.
guesses.why: 30.Kd2! The king steps in front of the d-pawn and stops it for good. Now White's rooks are free to attack.

guesses.prompt: Two rooks on the seventh. Drive the king back with check.
guesses.hint: The rook on e7 can step sideways with check.
guesses.why: 32.Rf7+ pushes the king to e8 and keeps it on the back rank, where the rooks can build a net.

guesses.prompt: The king is on e8. Keep the rooks working together on the seventh rank.
guesses.hint: One rook moves to a square where it also eyes Black's pawns and the b-file.
guesses.why: 33.Rb7 keeps both rooks on the seventh, boxing the king in. If Black grabs the b4 pawn, the bishop joins the hunt.

steps.title: Knight for bishop
steps.question: Why did Fischer give his strong knight for Black's bishop on move 22?

options.text: A bishop is usually better than a knight in an open endgame with pawns on both sides
options.why: Right. The bishop can reach both wings quickly; the knight is slow.

options.text: Knights are worth less than bishops in every position
options.why: Not every position: in closed positions a knight can be better. Here the board was open.

options.text: He wanted to avoid a draw by repetition
options.why: There was no repetition. He chose the endgame he knew was easier to win.

steps.title: Trade into the right endgame
steps.text: Fischer did not keep his best-looking piece. He asked which endgame would be easiest to win and traded into it: bishop against knight, rooks on the seventh, king in the center. Good endgame players trade pieces on purpose, not just to simplify.
steps.narration: Do not keep a piece because it looks nice. Trade into the endgame you can win.
